title: Tanto gentile in the Vita Nuova
greek: Tanto gentile e tanto onesta pare / la donna mia quand'ella altrui saluta
short: Rossetti's version of 'Tanto gentile e tanto onesta pare', the sonnet of Beatrice's public praise, Vita Nuova ch. XXVI (Barbi).
body: In the prose that frames it, Dante describes how people ran to see Beatrice in the streets, how those she greeted could not raise their eyes, and how she went 'crowned and clothed with humility'. The sonnet is the summit of the 'praise style' (stilo de la loda) that Dante adopts in the middle of the Vita Nuova, after resolving to write only in praise of Beatrice rather than of his own suffering. Barbi numbers the chapter XXVI; Gorni's edition, chapter 17. Rossetti translated the whole Vita Nuova as a young man (chiefly 1845-49) and published it in The Early Italian Poets (1861). Robert Pogue Harrison calls the poem pivotal, the point where Beatrice's greeting becomes redemptive.

sources.cite: Dante Alighieri, La Vita Nuova, ed. Michele Barbi (Florence: Bemporad, Società Dantesca Italiana, 1932), ch. XXVI

title: looks (pare)
short: Dante's 'pare' does not mean 'seems' but 'appears visibly, is manifest'; Rossetti's 'looks' and 'Seeming' follow the modern sense.
body: Gianfranco Contini's famous essay of 1947 showed that almost every key word of this sonnet has shifted meaning since Dante. 'Parere', here and in 'par che sia' (l. 7) and 'par che... si mova' (l. 12), means 'to show itself, to be evidently': Beatrice does not merely seem noble, her nobility is made manifest. Rossetti, like most nineteenth-century readers, renders it as appearance ('looks', 'Seeming', 'there seems'), which introduces a note of doubt that Dante's lines do not have. The repeated verb ties the poem to its theme of manifestation and miracle.

sources.cite: Gianfranco Contini, 'Esercizio d'interpretazione sopra un sonetto di Dante' (1947), repr. in Un'idea di Dante (Turin: Einaudi, 1976)
Donato Pirovano, 'Lettura di Tanto gentile e tanto onesta pare' (University of Turin, open-access PDF)

title: gentle and so pure (gentile, onesta)
short: 'Gentile' means noble in the stilnovo sense, nobility of heart; 'onesta' means dignified, decorous (Latin honestus), not 'honest' or 'pure'.
body: Gentilezza, nobility of soul as opposed to birth, was the central value of the dolce stil novo, theorised in Guinizzelli's canzone 'Al cor gentil' and in Dante's 'Amore e 'l cor gentil sono una cosa' (VN XX). 'Onesta' derives from Latin honestas, outward dignity and seemliness that reveals inner worth. Contini stressed that both describe what appears in public, matching 'pare'. Rossetti's 'gentle and so pure' is beautiful but moves toward modern softness and moral purity, a characteristic Victorian shading.

sources.cite: Gianfranco Contini, 'Esercizio d'interpretazione sopra un sonetto di Dante' (1947), repr. in Un'idea di Dante (Turin: Einaudi, 1976)

title: salutation (saluto / salute)
short: Translates 'quand'ella altrui saluta': in the Vita Nuova Beatrice's greeting (saluto) is also salvation (salute).
body: Earlier in the Vita Nuova (chs. III, X-XI) Beatrice's greeting brings the poet a bliss beyond which he desires nothing, and her denial of it plunges him into grief. Dante plays on saluto (greeting) and salute (health, salvation), both from Latin salus. The greeting is thus a quasi-sacramental act. Rossetti's 'yielding salutation by the way' keeps the formality but not the pun, which English cannot carry; his 'by the way' (in the street) comes from the prose context.

sources.cite: Dante Alighieri, La Vita Nuova, ed. Michele Barbi (Florence: Bemporad, Società Dantesca Italiana, 1932), ch. XXVI

title: the tongue trembles
short: Translates 'ch'ogne lingua deven tremando muta': every tongue becomes trembling and mute, the inexpressibility of her effect.
body: The speechless, trembling beholder is a stilnovo topos; Cavalcanti's sonnet 'Chi è questa che vèn' (in the archive in Rossetti's version) says that in her presence 'none / Dare speak'. Dante's 'ogne lingua', every tongue, makes the effect universal, not just the lover's. Rossetti's 'the tongue' and 'has nought to say' soften the generalisation slightly. Critics often read the whole sonnet as Dante's answer to Cavalcanti's: the same effects, but turned from anguish to blessing.

sources.cite: Teodolinda Barolini, Dante's Lyric Poetry: Poems of Youth and of the 'Vita Nuova', trans. Richard Lansing (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2014), commentary on 'Tanto gentile' (VN XXVI [17])
Robert Pogue Harrison, 'Saved by a Vision of Beatrice', New York Review of Books, 26 May 2011
Rossetti Archive, commentary on 'Chi è questa, che ven, ch'ogni uom la mira' (Cavalcanti; Rossetti's 1861 translation)

title: may not endure
greek: e li occhi no l'ardiscon di guardare
short: Translates 'e li occhi no l'ardiscon di guardare': the eyes do not dare to look at her.
body: Dante's verb is 'ardire', to dare: the beholder's eyes are overcome by reverence. Rossetti's 'may not endure' suggests rather a physical dazzlement, as before the sun. Both senses belong to the tradition in which the lady's light is too strong for mortal sight. 'Fain' in Rossetti's line means 'gladly, willingly' (OED, fain, adv.). The prose of the chapter makes the same point in narrative form: those whom she greeted lowered their eyes and could not answer her.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'fain, adv.'

title: secure
short: 'Secure' keeps its Latin sense, 'free from care, untroubled': Beatrice hears herself praised without vanity or anxiety.
body: Dante's line is 'Ella si va, sentendosi laudare': she goes on her way hearing herself praised. Rossetti's 'secure' (Latin securus, from se- 'without' and cura 'care') adds an interpretation: the praise does not disturb her (OED, secure, adj., sense 1). The motif of public praise defines the 'stilo de la loda', the new style announced in Vita Nuova XVIII-XIX with the canzone 'Donne ch'avete intelletto d'amore' (in the archive as 'Ladies that have intelligence in love').

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'secure, adj.'

title: humbleness for her array
short: Translates 'benignamente d'umiltà vestuta', graciously clothed in humility, a Marian image.
body: Humility as a garment recalls the language of devotion to the Virgin, who in the Magnificat praises God for regarding 'the low estate [humilitatem] of his handmaiden' (Luke 1:48). Umiltà in Dante's usage also has the sense of benign graciousness, not self-abasement. Rossetti drops 'benignamente' and turns the clothing image into 'array', apparel. The prose of the chapter repeats the phrase, saying she went 'crowned and clothed with humility'.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Luke 1:48
Teodolinda Barolini, Dante's Lyric Poetry: Poems of Youth and of the 'Vita Nuova', trans. Richard Lansing (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2014), commentary on 'Tanto gentile' (VN XXVI [17])

title: a miracle made sure
short: Translates 'e par che sia una cosa venuta / da cielo in terra a miracol mostrare': come from heaven to earth to show a miracle.
body: These lines make Beatrice a revelation: she has come down to earth to demonstrate a miracle, an image with Christological overtones (Harrison speaks of her as a Christ-like figure). Later in the Vita Nuova (XXIX) Dante says that she was herself 'a nine', a miracle whose root is the Trinity. In Contini's reading 'par' here again means 'evidently is', so the miracle is shown rather than suggested. Rossetti's 'Seeming' and 'made sure' (made certain, demonstrated) pull in opposite directions; 'made sure' is close to 'mostrare', but 'Seeming' introduces doubt.

anchor: She is so pleasant in the eyes of men
title: the sestet
greek: Mostrasi sì piacente a chi la mira
short: The sestet begins 'Mostrasi sì piacente a chi la mira': she shows herself so pleasing to whoever beholds her.
body: 'Mostrasi' (she shows herself) continues the chain of 'pare' and 'mostrare': the poem is entirely about appearance in the strong sense of manifestation. In Dante the sestet rhymes CDE EDC (mira, core, prova; mova, amore, sospira). Rossetti's sestet uses rhymes of his own (men, gain, by; move, love, Sigh), with 'move/love' an eye-rhyme, and indents some lines in the manner of the 1861 printing. His octave keeps Dante's ABBA ABBA. 'Pleasant' renders 'piacente', which has the stronger sense of 'pleasing, delightful'.

sources.cite: Dante Alighieri, La Vita Nuova, ed. Michele Barbi (Florence: Bemporad, Società Dantesca Italiana, 1932), ch. XXVI

anchor: through the sight the inmost heart
title: through the sight to the heart
greek: per li occhi una dolcezza al core
short: Translates 'che dà per li occhi una dolcezza al core': love's sweetness passes through the eyes to the heart.
body: The physiology of love in the Middle Ages, from Andreas Capellanus to the stilnovisti, held that love is born of sight: an image enters through the eyes and descends to the heart. Here, however, what passes is not desire but 'dolcezza', sweetness, a gift rather than a wound. Harrison notes that a modern translation which omits the heart and the soul loses the poem's spiritual physiology; Rossetti keeps both.

sources.cite: Robert Pogue Harrison, 'Saved by a Vision of Beatrice', New York Review of Books, 26 May 2011
Teodolinda Barolini, Dante's Lyric Poetry: Poems of Youth and of the 'Vita Nuova', trans. Richard Lansing (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2014), commentary on 'Tanto gentile' (VN XXVI [17])

anchor: needs proof to know it by
title: known only by experience
greek: che 'ntender no la può chi no la prova
short: Translates 'che 'ntender no la può chi no la prova': no one can understand it who has not experienced it.
body: The appeal to experience (prova) is a lyric topos: only lovers understand love. Petrarch uses the same word in Rvf 1 ('ove sia chi per prova intenda amore'). Rossetti's line keeps the logic but his 'needs proof to know it by' is compressed to the point of obscurity: it means 'requires to be experienced in order to be known'. The thought also anticipates the Paradiso's insistence that the highest experiences exceed telling.

sources.cite: Teodolinda Barolini, Dante's Lyric Poetry: Poems of Youth and of the 'Vita Nuova', trans. Richard Lansing (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2014), commentary on 'Tanto gentile' (VN XXVI [17])

Donato Pirovano, 'Lettura di Tanto gentile e tanto onesta pare' (University of Turin, open-access PDF)

title: lips... a soothing essence
short: Dante: 'e par che de la sua labbia si mova / un spirito soave pien d'amore'. Both 'labbia' and 'spirito' need care.
body: 'Labbia' in Dante often means the face or countenance, not the lips (compare Inferno 7.7, 'quella 'nfiata labbia', 'that swollen face'); Rossetti's 'from between her lips' takes the narrower sense, and editors differ. 'Spirito' belongs to the medical-philosophical doctrine of spirits, the subtle vapours that carried perception and emotion between eye, heart and brain, which Cavalcanti uses obsessively. Rossetti's 'essence' blurs this technical sense into something more Victorian and ethereal. In Dante the spirit 'si mova', moves, from her face to the beholder's soul.

sources.cite: Gianfranco Contini, 'Esercizio d'interpretazione sopra un sonetto di Dante' (1947), repr. in Un'idea di Dante (Turin: Einaudi, 1976)

anchor: Saying for ever to the spirit
title: the final 'Sigh!'
greek: che va dicendo a l'anima: Sospira
short: Dante ends on 'che va dicendo a l'anima: Sospira', which goes saying to the soul, 'Sigh!'
body: The poem closes on a single imperative word. In Cavalcanti the sigh is the sign of love's destructive power; Harrison argues that here it is instead a sigh of spiritual infusion, full of hope rather than despair, and that this marks Dante's break from Cavalcanti's influence. Rossetti renders 'anima' (soul) as 'spirit', which confuses it with the 'spirito' of line 13, and adds 'for ever', making the effect perpetual. Many readers consider this the most perfect sonnet of the Vita Nuova.

sources.cite: Robert Pogue Harrison, 'Saved by a Vision of Beatrice', New York Review of Books, 26 May 2011
